description:
Jackets to keep the rain out. A waterproof is the outer layer you pull on when the weather turns, worn over a base layer or fleece so you can add or remove warmth underneath as the day changes.

For cold, dry days, see Insulated Jackets. For wind and light showers on the move, see Softshell Jackets.

Insulated jackets are for warmth rather than rain: the layer you put on at camp, on a winter walk or at a lunch stop, when you stop moving and cool down quickly.

In wet weather, wear a waterproof over the top. See Waterproof Jackets.

Softshell jackets sit between a fleece and a waterproof. They suit active days that are windy, cool or showery rather than properly wet, when you want to keep moving without overheating.

If heavy rain is forecast, a waterproof shell is the better choice.
Fleeces are the warm middle layer: over a base layer, under a waterproof, or on their own on a dry day. Easy to pack into a rucksack for the top of the hill or the evening at camp.

Walking boots for hill walking, long days on rough paths and wet, muddy ground, where you want more support around the ankle than a shoe gives.

Pair them with a good pair of walking socks. For lighter, faster walking on drier trails, see Trail Shoes.

Trail shoes are the lighter option to a walking boot: low-cut footwear for well-made paths, day walks and quicker trips on drier ground.

Heading onto rougher or boggier terrain? See Walking Boots.
Wellies for wet fields, muddy campsites, dog walks and festivals. Pull them on for short trips through standing water and mud rather than long days on the hill.

Tents for camping trips, from a night or two on your own to a longer stay at a campsite. Choose by how many people will sleep in it and how you'll carry it there.

Complete your sleep system with a sleeping bag and a sleeping mat.

Walking boots for hill walking, long days on rough paths and wet, muddy ground, where you want more support around the ankle than a shoe gives.

Wear them with proper walking socks. For lighter, faster walking on drier trails, see Trail Shoes.

Sleeping bags for summer camping and for colder nights. Pick one for the lowest temperature you expect to sleep in, and put a sleeping mat underneath: much of the cold at night comes up from the ground.

Foam and self-inflating sleeping mats. A mat is what stops the ground drawing heat out of you overnight, so it matters as much as the sleeping bag on top of it.

Foam mats are simple and hard to damage; self-inflating mats pack smaller and are more comfortable.
Gas stoves, fuel and pans for cooking at camp, from a brew on a day walk to evening meals on a longer trip.

Daypacks for a day on the hill, and bigger rucksacks for multi-day trips with a tent and sleeping bag to carry. A good fit makes more difference than any feature, so see our rucksack fitting guide before you choose.
Rechargeable head torches that leave both hands free, for walks that finish after dark, early starts and finding your way around a tent at night.
The kit that goes with you on every walk or camping trip: rucksacks, head torches, walking poles, water bottles, hats, gloves, and maps and guides.
Folding camping chairs for sitting in comfort at the campsite, around the stove in the evening, or at the beach and festivals.
Cool boxes to keep food and drinks cold on camping trips, picnics and days out in the car.
Walking poles take some of the load off your knees on steep descents and help your balance on rough or slippery ground. Many walkers use a pair on long days in the hills.
Water bottles for walks, runs and camping trips. Keep one in the side pocket of your rucksack so a drink is always in reach.
Walking socks to wear with walking boots and trail shoes. The right pair cushions your feet and helps prevent blisters on long days.

Walking poles take some of the load off your knees on steep descents and help your balance on rough or slippery ground. They are usually used in pairs and fold or telescope down to strap onto a rucksack.
Outdoor clothing for walking and camping, built up in layers: base layers next to the skin, fleeces for warmth, and jackets for rain, wind and cold. Choose a section below.
Footwear for the outdoors: walking boots for hills and rough ground, trail shoes for lighter walking, wellies for mud and wet fields, and walking socks to go with them.
Everything for a night or more under canvas: tents, sleeping bags and mats to sleep on, stoves to cook on, and chairs and cool boxes for the campsite.
Outdoor jackets by type: waterproof jackets for rain, insulated jackets for cold, softshells for active days in changeable weather, and jackets for kids.

Base layers are the first layer you put on, worn next to the skin under a fleece or jacket. Their job is to move sweat away from your body so you stay warm and dry while you're active.

For wool rather than synthetic, see Merino Base Layers.
Warm, dry jackets for children, for school runs, family walks and days out in wet or cold weather.
Base layers made from merino wool, a soft, fine wool that stays warm when damp and is less prone to smelling after a day's wear than most synthetics. A good choice for multi-day trips.
Hats for walking and camping: warm hats for winter and cold evenings at camp, and sun hats for summer days on the hill.
Gloves to keep your hands warm on cold walks and winter days out, when you still need to hold walking poles, a map or a phone.
OS maps at 1:25,000 scale, the detailed scale most walkers use for planning routes and navigating on the hill, along with walking guides.
